q-15687.name: Question 1
q-15687.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14275039/assets/339662001ca92041da1f2d3531c3e841e987a7eff256d5ead1d23255ccee238a.png)

Find the $x$-intercepts of the circle $(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=20,$ shown above.
q-15687.worked_solution:
We must have $y=0$ at the $x$-intercepts. 

So, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the circle and solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =20 \\ (x-2)^{2}+(0-2)^{2} & =20 \\ (x-2)^{2}+4 & =20 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =16 \\ x-2 & =\pm \sqrt{16} \\ x & =2\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercepts occur at the points $(-2,0)$ and $(6,0).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14275039/assets/c6d356b443128da569a6b60065769cdb56e2e0059db7b146a3c4035d18a32228.png)

Find the $x$-intercepts of the circle $(x-1)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=45,$ shown above.
q-15684.worked_solution:
We must have $y=0$ at the $x$-intercepts. 

So, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the circle and solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} & =45 \\ (x-1)^{2}+(0-3)^{2} & =45 \\ (x-1)^{2}+9 & =45 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =36 \\ x-1 & =\pm \sqrt{36} \\ x & =1\pm 6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercepts occur at the points $(-5,0)$ and $(7,0).$

q-15684.html:
Question 2
?

Find the x-intercepts of the circle (x−1)2+(y−3)2=45, shown above.

a
(−6,0) and (8,0)
b
(−6,0) and (7,0)
c
(−5,0) and (8,0)
d
(−5,0) and (7,0)
e
(−5.5,0) and (7.5,0)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We must have y=0 at the x-intercepts.

So, we need to substitute y=0 into the equation of the circle and solve for x, as follows: (x−1)2+(y−3)2=45(x−1)2+(0−3)2=45(x−1)2+9=45(x−1)2=36x−1=±36x=1±6

Therefore, the x-intercepts occur at the points (−5,0) and (7,0).

q-8794.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4x-2y+1 & =0 \\ {0}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4\cdot 0-2y+1 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-2y+1 & =0 \\ (y-1)^{2} & =0 \\ y-1 & =0 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}

q-15705.worked_solution:
We must have $x=0$ at the $y$-intercepts. 

So, we need to substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the circle and solve for $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =20 \\ (0-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =20 \\ 4+(y-2)^{2} & =20 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =16 \\ y-2 & =\pm \sqrt{16} \\ y & =2\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $y$-intercepts occur at the points $(0,-2)$ and $(0,6).$

q-160275.name: Question 5
q-160275.worked_solution:
When the circle intercepts the $y$-axis, we must have $x=0.$

So, we need to substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for $y$, if possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2}+(y+2)^{2} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ (0+1)^{2}+(y+2)^{2} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ 1+(y+2)^{2} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ (y+2)^{2} & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(y+2)^{2}\ge 0$ for all values of $y,$ there is no $y$ such that $(y+2)^{2}=-\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore, the circle does not intercept the $y$-axis at any point, as shown below.

Calculate the y-intercepts of the circle (x+1)2+(y+2)2=34.

(x+1)2+(y+2)2=34(0+1)2+(y+2)2=341+(y+2)2=34(y+2)2=−14.

q-160284.name: Question 6
q-160284.worked_solution:
We must have $x=0$ at the $y$-intercepts.  

So, we need to substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for $y,$ if possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6x-6y+14 & =0 \\ {0}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6\cdot 0-6y+14 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-6y+14 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this equation by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-6y+9+14 & =0+9 \\ (y-3)^{2}+14 & =9 \\ (y-3)^{2} & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(y-3)^{2}\ge 0$ for all values of $y,$ there is no $y$ such that $(y-3)^{2}=-5.$ Therefore, circle has no $y$-intercepts, as shown below.

Question 6

Calculate the y-intercepts of the circle x2+y2−6x−6y+14=0

a
(0,3)
b
(0,1) and (0,5)
c
(0,−1) and (0,7)
d
(0,−3)
e
The circle has no y-intercepts
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We must have x=0 at the y-intercepts.

So, we need to substitute x=0 into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for y, if possible:

x2+y2−6x−6y+14=002+y2−6⋅0−6y+14=0y2−6y+14=0

We can solve this equation by completing the square, as follows:

y2−6y+9+14=0+9(y−3)2+14=9(y−3)2=−5

Since (y−3)2≥0 for all values of y, there is no y such that (y−3)2=−5. Therefore, circle has no y-intercepts, as shown below.
